citations.title: What Site and due diligence evidence cannot establish
citations.location: Operator guidance: evidence-limits; section What Site and due diligence cannot establish; chars 1-1098
citations.excerpt:
# What Site and due diligence cannot establish

The evidence here is a record of what was gathered for a property, not a determination about it.
Recording that a control, hazard or building matter was checked is not the same as certifying the
property against it. A site review is not a building inspection, a planning certificate, a survey
or legal advice, however complete it looks.

## Questions this feature cannot answer

Site and due diligence cannot tell you whether a property complies with a planning control or the
Building Code, whether it is safe or structurally sound, whether a past change was approved, or
whether it is a suitable purchase. It cannot value the property, assess contract terms, or say
whether a price is fair.

Those determinations belong to the relevant authority or a licensed professional: a certifier or
council for compliance, a building inspector or engineer for condition, a surveyor for boundaries,
and a conveyancer or lawyer for title and contract. Questions about recorded sale prices or market
value belong to the Sales and market research area, not here.

citations.location: Operator guidance: evidence-limits; section Demonstration data; chars 1714-2085
citations.excerpt:
## Demonstration data

Some reviews include deterministic synthetic showcase evidence so the workflow can be demonstrated
without real records. Where that is so, treat those figures as an illustration of the mechanics
only. They must never be quoted as evidence about a real property, and no conclusion about an
actual site, building or approval should be drawn from them.

citations.title: What Site and due diligence does and does not claim
citations.location: Operator guidance: what-this-feature-does; section How to record a site review; chars 1473-2072
citations.excerpt:
## How to record a site review

Choose New review, select the property by its address, confirm it is the one you meant, and give
the review a title. Set its status as you progress, for example draft while you are still gathering
evidence.

Work through the checklist for the planning, environmental, strata and building matters that apply,
and add notes that explain what you found or still need to confirm. When you are ready, ask the
assistant to generate professional-verification questions; it grounds them in the evidence states
and prioritises whatever is unavailable or only partially covered.

citations.title: How due-diligence evidence is classified and how confident that is
citations.location: Operator guidance: evidence-states; section Reading a due-diligence summary honestly; chars 1019-1627
citations.excerpt:
## Reading a due-diligence summary honestly

Read confirmed evidence alongside what is unavailable or only partially covered. A review that
looks reassuring because little was flagged may simply have many unavailable sources, and those
gaps are the priority to verify, not a clean result.

For that reason the assistant prioritises questions about unavailable and partial-coverage evidence
when it builds a verification pack. A non-intersection result reduces concern about that specific
hazard layer but does not close the matter, and it says nothing about controls or building records
held by other sources.

citations.title: What Site and due diligence does and does not claim
citations.location: Operator guidance: what-this-feature-does; section What Site and due diligence does; chars 1-605
citations.excerpt:
# What Site and due diligence does

Site and due diligence is a pre-purchase research workspace for one property at a time. You record
a site review against a verified property, gather the planning, environmental, strata and building
evidence held for it, work through a due-diligence checklist, and turn the gaps into clear
questions a buyer can put to a suitably qualified professional.

It is research support. It does not certify that a property complies with any control, confirm it
is safe or structurally sound, decide whether it is legally suitable, or replace advice from a
licensed professional.
